stem: In biometrics, what is a Type I error?

options.A: A legitimate user is wrongly rejected
options.B: An impostor is wrongly accepted as a legitimate user
options.C: The system records the wrong time for an authentication attempt
options.D: The reader fails to capture any sample from the user at all

explanation: A Type I error is a false rejection: the system refuses a valid user. A Type II error is a false acceptance.

distractor_rationales.B: Wrongly accepting an impostor is a Type II error, or false acceptance.
distractor_rationales.C: Timestamp errors are unrelated to biometric error types.
distractor_rationales.D: A failure to capture is a separate metric, not a Type I error.

references_topic: Type I and Type II biometric errors

stem: An authenticator app shows a six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds. What type of one-time password is this?

options.A: HMAC-based one-time password that advances only when a button is pressed
options.B: Time-based one-time password (TOTP)
options.C: Static password stored in the app's settings
options.D: Knowledge-based answer to a security question

explanation: TOTP codes are derived from a shared secret and the current time, so they change at a fixed interval.

distractor_rationales.A: HOTP codes advance with a counter, such as a button press, not with time.
distractor_rationales.C: A static password does not change every 30 seconds.
distractor_rationales.D: Security question answers are knowledge factors that do not change.

stem: Which property is MOST important for a web session identifier?

options.A: It should include the user's name so support staff can read it easily
options.B: It should be short, so that it loads faster in the browser
options.C: It should be long and generated by a secure random number generator
options.D: It should stay the same for each user across every session they start

explanation: A session ID must be unpredictable so attackers cannot guess or calculate valid ones. Length and a cryptographically secure random source provide that.

distractor_rationales.A: Readable user data makes IDs easier to guess and leaks information.
distractor_rationales.B: Short IDs are easier to brute-force.
distractor_rationales.D: Reusing the same ID enables session fixation and replay.

stem: What is identity proofing?

options.A: Checking a password against a stored hash each time a user signs in
options.B: Granting a user the specific set of permissions that their job role requires
options.C: Recording what a user does after they have been authenticated
options.D: Verifying a person is who they claim to be before issuing credentials

explanation: Identity proofing establishes that a claimed identity belongs to the real person, for example by checking documents, before an account and credentials are created.

distractor_rationales.A: Password checking is authentication.
distractor_rationales.B: Assigning permissions is authorization.
distractor_rationales.C: Recording activity is accounting.

stem: With single sign-on, one stolen credential could open every connected application. What BEST reduces this risk?

options.A: Strong, phishing-resistant MFA and conditional access at the identity provider
options.B: Longer SSO sessions so that users sign in less often and see far fewer MFA prompts
options.C: Separate passwords for each application in addition to the SSO login
options.D: Turning off logging at the identity provider to protect user privacy

explanation: SSO concentrates access, so the identity provider must be strongly protected. Phishing-resistant MFA and context-aware policies make one stolen password far less useful.

distractor_rationales.B: Longer sessions increase the value of a stolen session.
distractor_rationales.C: Extra passwords undo the benefits of SSO and encourage password reuse.
distractor_rationales.D: Logging is needed to detect misuse.

stem: A new application role was created, but no permissions have been assigned to it yet. What should a user who holds only this role be able to access?

options.A: Everything, until someone adds restrictions
options.B: Nothing
options.C: Whatever the previous user of the role could access
options.D: Only the data that other users have marked as public

explanation: Access control should default to deny. Without an explicit grant, the role should give no access.

distractor_rationales.A: Default allow exposes everything until someone notices.
distractor_rationales.C: Roles do not inherit access from previous users.
distractor_rationales.D: Access should come from explicit grants, not assumptions about public data.

stem: Which system should normally be the authoritative source that triggers joiner, mover, and leaver account changes?

options.A: The help desk ticketing system where users request access
options.B: Each application's own local user database
options.C: The HR system of record
options.D: The email server's distribution lists

explanation: The HR system knows when people are hired, change roles, or leave, so automated provisioning driven by it keeps accounts aligned with employment status.

distractor_rationales.A: Tickets capture requests, not authoritative employment status.
distractor_rationales.B: Local databases are what provisioning should update, not the source.
distractor_rationales.D: Distribution lists are not authoritative for employment status.

stem: Which access should an organization review MOST often?

options.A: Read access to the public company intranet
options.B: Membership in company-wide email distribution lists
options.C: Access to the cafeteria menu and parking systems
options.D: Privileged and administrative access to critical systems

explanation: Review frequency should follow risk. Privileged access to critical systems can cause the most harm if misused, so it deserves the closest and most frequent review.

distractor_rationales.A: Public intranet access is low risk.
distractor_rationales.B: Distribution list membership is low risk.
distractor_rationales.C: Cafeteria and parking systems are low risk.

stem: Why do privileged access management tools often record administrator sessions?

options.A: To provide accountability and evidence of what was done with elevated rights
options.B: To make administrator sessions run faster on slow network connections
options.C: To replace the need for multi-factor authentication for all of the administrators
options.D: To allow administrators to share one account without any confusion

explanation: Recordings show exactly what happened during privileged sessions, which deters misuse and supports investigations and audits.

distractor_rationales.B: Recording does not speed up sessions.
distractor_rationales.C: Recording complements MFA; it does not replace it.
distractor_rationales.D: Shared accounts undermine accountability even with recording.

stem: In Kerberos, which two services make up the key distribution center?

options.A: The relying party and the identity provider
options.B: The authentication service and the ticket-granting service
options.C: The policy decision point and the policy enforcement point together
options.D: The RADIUS client and the RADIUS server

explanation: The KDC contains the authentication service, which issues ticket-granting tickets, and the ticket-granting service, which issues service tickets.

distractor_rationales.A: Relying parties and identity providers are federation roles.
distractor_rationales.C: Decision and enforcement points are access policy components.
distractor_rationales.D: RADIUS is a separate AAA protocol.

stem: A tester cloned several employee badges in seconds with a cheap reader held near their pockets. The badges are older 125 kHz proximity cards. What is the BEST fix?

options.A: Print a hologram on each badge to make visual copies harder to create
options.B: Ask employees to keep their badges in a shirt pocket instead of a trouser pocket
options.C: Replace them with encrypted smart cards that use mutual authentication
options.D: Require employees to show their badge to a guard at the front desk each day

explanation: Older proximity cards transmit a fixed ID with no cryptography, so they are easy to clone. Smart cards with cryptographic challenge and response cannot be copied that way.

distractor_rationales.A: A hologram does not stop radio cloning.
distractor_rationales.B: Pocket location does not prevent close-range reading.
distractor_rationales.D: A visual check does not detect a cloned card presented at a reader.

stem: The company forces password changes every 60 days with complex composition rules, and users write their passwords on notes. What is the BEST policy change?

options.A: Shorten the change interval to 30 days so that written passwords expire sooner
options.B: Add more composition rules so that passwords become even harder to guess
options.C: Allow users to reuse their previous passwords so they are easier to remember
options.D: Favor longer passphrases, block breached passwords, and change only on compromise

explanation: Current guidance favors length and screening against known-breached passwords over frequent forced changes, which lead to weak, predictable patterns and written notes.

distractor_rationales.A: More frequent changes make the problem worse.
distractor_rationales.B: More rules increase the burden and the note-writing.
distractor_rationales.C: Reuse lets compromised passwords stay valid.

stem: Every user must use MFA for web sign-in, yet attackers are logging in to mailboxes with stolen passwords alone through older email protocols. What is the BEST fix?

options.A: Disable legacy authentication protocols that cannot perform MFA
options.B: Force users to change their passwords more often
options.C: Add a warning banner to the web sign-in page
options.D: Increase the MFA prompt timeout to reduce user complaints

explanation: Older protocols such as basic-authentication IMAP or POP accept only a password, bypassing MFA. Disabling them closes the gap.

distractor_rationales.B: Password changes do not stop protocols that bypass MFA.
distractor_rationales.C: A banner on the web page does not affect other protocols.
distractor_rationales.D: The timeout is unrelated to protocols that skip MFA.

stem: A tester logs out of a web application, then replays the old session cookie and is still logged in. What is the BEST fix?

options.A: Delete the cookie from the browser when the user clicks the logout button
options.B: Invalidate the session on the server when the user logs out
options.C: Encrypt the cookie so that the tester cannot read its contents
options.D: Shorten the cookie's name so that it is harder to find in the browser

explanation: Logout must end the session on the server. Removing the cookie only in the browser leaves the server-side session valid for anyone holding a copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Browser deletion does not stop a copied cookie from being used.
distractor_rationales.C: An encrypted cookie can still be replayed.
distractor_rationales.D: The cookie's name does not affect its validity.

stem: In a service provider-initiated SAML sign-in, what happens first after the user tries to open the application?

options.A: The identity provider sends a signed assertion directly to the application without any user interaction
options.B: The user types their password into the application's own login form
options.C: The application redirects the user to the identity provider with an authentication request
options.D: The application asks the user's browser to generate a new certificate

explanation: The service provider sends the browser to the identity provider with an authentication request. After the user signs in, the IdP returns a signed assertion to the service provider.

distractor_rationales.A: In SP-initiated flow the assertion follows the request and user sign-in.
distractor_rationales.B: With federation, the application does not collect the user's password.
distractor_rationales.D: Browsers do not create certificates as part of SAML sign-in.

stem: In an access control matrix, subjects are rows and objects are columns. Which structure lists everything a single subject can access?

options.A: An access control list attached to an object
options.B: A security label on each file
options.C: A role definition in the directory
options.D: A capability list

explanation: A capability list is a row of the matrix: one subject and all its rights. An access control list is a column: one object and every subject's rights to it.

distractor_rationales.A: An ACL is tied to an object, not to a subject.
distractor_rationales.B: Security labels support mandatory access control, not the matrix row.
distractor_rationales.C: A role groups permissions but is not the matrix row for a subject.

stem: In a mandatory access control system, a user with a Secret clearance tries to open a Secret document in a project compartment they are not assigned to. What happens?

options.A: Access is denied, since clearance alone does not grant need to know for the compartment
options.B: Access is granted, since the user's clearance matches the document's classification
options.C: Access is granted, but only in read-only mode for the rest of the day
options.D: The document's owner decides at their discretion whether to allow access

explanation: Under MAC with compartments, access requires both sufficient clearance and membership in the compartment, which enforces need to know.

distractor_rationales.B: Matching clearance is necessary but not sufficient.
distractor_rationales.C: MAC does not grant partial access to unauthorized compartments.
distractor_rationales.D: Owner discretion describes DAC, not MAC.

references_topic: Need to know in MAC compartments

stem: Forty internal applications each implement their own access rules in code, and audits keep finding inconsistencies. What is the BEST long-term approach?

options.A: Ask each development team to write down its rules in a shared spreadsheet
options.B: Move authorization decisions into a central policy engine the apps call
options.C: Remove access checks from the applications and rely on the network firewall
options.D: Review the source code of all forty applications once every few years

explanation: A central policy decision point applies consistent rules that can be reviewed in one place, while each application enforces the returned decisions.

distractor_rationales.A: Documentation does not make the code consistent.
distractor_rationales.C: Network firewalls cannot enforce application-level permissions.
distractor_rationales.D: Infrequent reviews leave inconsistencies in place for years.

stem: Leavers are disabled in the corporate directory, but many keep working logins to SaaS tools that use local accounts. What is the BEST fix?

options.A: Ask each SaaS vendor to send a monthly list of active accounts to the security team
options.B: Remind managers to email every SaaS administrator when an employee leaves
options.C: Connect the SaaS tools to SSO and automated provisioning such as SCIM
options.D: Change the corporate directory password policy to require longer passwords

explanation: Federating sign-in removes separate passwords, and automated provisioning through standards such as SCIM removes accounts when the directory changes.

distractor_rationales.A: Monthly reports leave access open for weeks.
distractor_rationales.B: Manual emails are unreliable.
distractor_rationales.D: Password length does not remove SaaS accounts.

stem: Administrators use one account for email, web browsing, and domain administration. What is the BEST change?

options.A: Require administrators to change that single account's password every month
options.B: Block administrators from receiving any email from outside the company
options.C: Give administrators a second computer but keep the same single account
options.D: Issue separate privileged accounts used only for administrative tasks

explanation: Separating daily and administrative identities means a phishing email or malicious site compromises only an ordinary account, not domain admin rights.

distractor_rationales.A: Frequent changes do not separate risky activity from privilege.
distractor_rationales.B: Blocking external email is disproportionate and does not address browsing.
distractor_rationales.C: A second computer with the same account keeps privilege exposed.

stem: Every workstation has the same local administrator password, so one compromised laptop lets an attacker log in to all the others. What is the BEST fix?

options.A: Use a tool that sets a unique, rotated local admin password on each machine
options.B: Rename the local administrator account on every workstation to "backup"
options.C: Change the shared local administrator password once each year
options.D: Disable the host firewall on workstations so that administrators can reach them

explanation: A local administrator password solution gives each machine its own random password, stored securely and rotated, which stops lateral movement with one reused credential.

distractor_rationales.B: Renaming does not change the shared password.
distractor_rationales.C: Annual changes still leave one password across all machines.
distractor_rationales.D: Disabling firewalls increases exposure.

stem: A tester captured NTLM authentication attempts on the network and relayed them to file servers to gain access. Which control BEST prevents this?

options.A: Increasing the length of Kerberos ticket lifetimes
options.B: Requiring SMB signing and reducing NTLM use in favor of Kerberos
options.C: Moving file servers to a different building on the same network
options.D: Disabling logging on the file servers to hide them from attackers

explanation: Relay attacks forward authentication to another server. SMB signing makes relayed sessions fail, and reducing NTLM removes the weaker protocol.

distractor_rationales.A: Kerberos ticket lifetime does not stop NTLM relay.
distractor_rationales.C: Physical location does not stop network relay.
distractor_rationales.D: Disabling logging hides attacks from defenders, not attackers.

stem: A production outage occurs at 3 a.m., and the only person who can approve just-in-time elevation is unreachable. What should the access design include?

options.A: Standing administrator rights for every on-call engineer to avoid this situation
options.B: A shared emergency password written in the on-call runbook
options.C: A defined emergency path with alerts and mandatory after-the-fact review
options.D: A rule that outages must wait until the approver is available

explanation: A pre-approved emergency path, which alerts security and is reviewed afterward, keeps operations running without falling back to standing privilege.

distractor_rationales.A: Standing rights defeat the purpose of just-in-time access.
distractor_rationales.B: A shared written password lacks accountability and control.
distractor_rationales.D: Waiting for approval during an outage harms the business.

stem: Attackers with stolen passwords are registering their own MFA devices on accounts that never enrolled one. What is the BEST control?

options.A: Send users a newsletter that describes the risks of MFA enrollment
options.B: Allow enrollment only from the company's office network during business hours
options.C: Remove MFA enrollment and fall back to passwords for those users
options.D: Require enrollment through a verified identity or pre-issued one-time code

explanation: Enrollment binds an authenticator to an identity. If a password alone allows enrollment, attackers can claim accounts, so enrollment must require stronger proof.

distractor_rationales.A: A newsletter does not stop attackers from enrolling.
distractor_rationales.B: Network location helps a little but insiders and compromised devices can still abuse it.
distractor_rationales.C: Removing MFA increases exposure.

stem: A user's account signs in to a workstation inside the headquarters building, but the badge system shows the user has not entered the building that day and HR records say they are on leave. What does this MOST likely indicate?

options.A: Someone else is using the user's credentials
options.B: The badge reader clock is slightly wrong
options.C: The user simply forgot to badge in when arriving
options.D: The workstation is running a scheduled task

explanation: When physical and logical records conflict, especially for someone on leave, credential misuse is the likely explanation and should be investigated.

distractor_rationales.B: A small clock error does not explain a full day with no entry.
distractor_rationales.C: Forgetting to badge is possible but unlikely for someone on leave.
distractor_rationales.D: A scheduled task does not produce an interactive sign-in by the user.

stem: An attacker stole a central database of employee fingerprint templates. What makes this breach especially serious, and what design BEST avoids it?

options.A: Fingerprints expire quickly; issue employees new fingerprints each year
options.B: Fingerprints cannot be changed; keep templates on user devices or secure hardware
options.C: Templates are public anyway; no change to the design is needed
options.D: Biometrics are always inaccurate; replace them with shared PIN codes

explanation: Unlike passwords, biometrics cannot be reissued. Matching on the user's device or in secure hardware, instead of storing templates centrally, limits the damage of a breach.

distractor_rationales.A: Fingerprints do not expire and cannot be reissued.
distractor_rationales.C: Stolen templates are sensitive and can aid spoofing.
distractor_rationales.D: Shared PINs are far weaker and lose individual accountability.

stem: Several users clicked "Accept" on a consent screen granting a malicious third-party app full access to their mailboxes. No passwords were stolen. What is the BEST response and prevention?

options.A: Reset the users' passwords, since that revokes all application access automatically
options.B: Enable MFA for the users, since the app should be blocked by MFA going forward
options.C: Revoke the grants and require admin approval for high-risk app permissions
options.D: Tell users to decline consent screens for the next month

explanation: Consent phishing abuses legitimate OAuth grants, which survive password resets and MFA. Revoking the grants and restricting user consent to low-risk scopes stops the abuse.

distractor_rationales.A: Password resets do not necessarily revoke OAuth tokens already granted.
distractor_rationales.B: MFA does not stop a user from granting consent.
distractor_rationales.D: Temporary advice does not revoke existing access or prevent future abuse.

stem: An API gateway caches authorization decisions for 24 hours. A user fired this morning can still call the API. What is the BEST fix?

options.A: Increase the cache time so that fewer calls reach the policy decision point
options.B: Ask the fired user to stop using the API until the cache expires
options.C: Move the policy decision point closer to the gateway on the network
options.D: Shorten the cache lifetime and flush cached decisions when access is revoked

explanation: Caching improves performance but delays revocation. Short lifetimes plus active invalidation when access changes make revocation take effect quickly.

distractor_rationales.A: Longer caching makes revocation slower.
distractor_rationales.B: Relying on the user is not a control.
distractor_rationales.C: Network placement does not change cached decisions.

stem: A former employee is rehired into a different department. The help desk reactivates their old account with all of its previous permissions. What should the process do instead?

options.A: Provision access based on the new role and remove the old entitlements
options.B: Keep the old permissions, since the employee already had them approved
options.C: Give the employee administrator rights until the new role is clearly defined
options.D: Create a second account and leave the old account active as a backup

explanation: Previous approvals relate to a job the person no longer holds. Access should be provisioned for the new role, with old entitlements removed, to prevent privilege creep.

distractor_rationales.B: Old approvals do not carry over to a new job.
distractor_rationales.C: Temporary admin rights are excessive.
distractor_rationales.D: Duplicate accounts complicate control and invite misuse.

stem: An access review finds a finance user who can both create vendors and approve payments in the ERP system. What is the BEST action?

options.A: Approve the access, since the user has had it for years without problems
options.B: Remove one of the conflicting rights, or add a compensating control if both are needed
options.C: Remove all of the user's access to the ERP system until the next review
options.D: Ask the user to promise not to approve payments to vendors they created

explanation: Holding both rights lets one person create a fake vendor and pay it. Removing one right restores separation of duties; if a small team makes that impossible, a compensating control such as independent review is needed.

distractor_rationales.A: A clean history does not remove the fraud risk.
distractor_rationales.C: Removing all access disrupts the user's legitimate work.
distractor_rationales.D: A promise is not a control.

references_topic: Separation of duties conflicts in reviews

stem: A web server is configured for unconstrained Kerberos delegation. What is the MAIN risk, and what is the BEST fix?

options.A: Tickets expire too quickly; extend ticket lifetimes on the domain controllers
options.B: The web server cannot authenticate users; enable NTLM as a fallback
options.C: If compromised, it can impersonate users to any service; use constrained delegation
options.D: Users see extra login prompts; disable Kerberos for the web server

explanation: Unconstrained delegation stores users' ticket-granting tickets on the server, so an attacker who controls it can act as those users anywhere. Constrained or resource-based delegation limits it to specific services.

distractor_rationales.A: Ticket lifetime is not the issue.
distractor_rationales.B: NTLM is weaker and does not address delegation risk.
distractor_rationales.D: Disabling Kerberos removes a stronger protocol.

stem: A just-in-time system grants full subscription owner rights for two hours whenever an engineer needs to restart a single virtual machine. What is the BEST improvement?

options.A: Shorten the elevation window to thirty minutes while keeping the same role
options.B: Remove the approval step to make the elevation process faster for engineers
options.C: Grant owner rights permanently, since the engineers need them so often
options.D: Offer task-scoped roles, such as VM operator, for each common request

explanation: Just-in-time access limits time, but least privilege also limits scope. Task-scoped roles give engineers only what each job needs, even during elevation.

distractor_rationales.A: A shorter window still grants excessive rights.
distractor_rationales.B: Removing approval weakens control without fixing scope.
distractor_rationales.C: Permanent owner rights create standing privilege.
